title: SQL
intro:
One tiny shop (`customers`, `orders`) on every card: a business question, the query, the real result (run in SQLite), one trap, and the next question.
Read the cards in order; the last one links to the [SQL cheat sheet](#cheat-sql).

sections.title: How to approach a question
sections.summary: A plan before typing: grain, columns, edge cases
sections.body:
**Question:** "Total spend per city." Where do you start?

Shop tables used on every card:

`customers`

| customer_id | name | city | signup_date |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Ana | Paris | 2024-01-05 |
| 2 | Ben | Rome | 2024-01-20 |
| 3 | Cara | Paris | 2024-02-10 |
| 4 | Dan | Rome | 2024-03-01 |

`orders`

| order_id | customer_id | order_date | amount |
|---|---|---|---|
| 101 | 1 | 2024-01-10 | 20 |
| 102 | 1 | 2024-02-15 | 300 |
| 103 | 2 | 2024-01-25 | 50 |
| 104 | 3 | 2024-02-12 | 10 |
| 105 | 1 | 2024-03-20 | 40 |
| 106 | 2 | 2024-03-02 | 50 |

**Plan:** 1) one output row per what? (city) 2) which columns? 3) which tables and keys? 4) write it 5) check edge cases (Dan has no orders, so Rome only counts Ben).

**Query:**
```sql
SELECT c.city, SUM(o.amount) AS spend
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
GROUP BY c.city;
```

**Result:**

| city | spend |
|---|---|
| Paris | 370 |
| Rome | 100 |

**Watch out:** say the plan out loud first: one row per city, columns city and spend, which tables, then edge cases (NULLs, ties, customers with no orders).

**Next question:** In what order does SQL actually run these lines? -> [Query order](#sql-query-order)
sections.explain:
Imagine your boss asks: "How much did each city spend?" Before typing, decide what one row of the answer is. Here it is one city, so the answer has two rows: Paris and Rome.

Now follow the database step by step. The city lives in `customers`, the money lives in `orders`, and `customer_id` connects them. The JOIN glues each order to its customer, so every order now also knows its city. Ana (Paris) has 20, 300 and 40, Cara (Paris) has 10, and Ben (Rome) has 50 and 50. GROUP BY city puts the Paris orders in one pile and the Rome orders in another. SUM adds each pile: Paris 20 + 300 + 40 + 10 = 370, Rome 50 + 50 = 100.

Dan lives in Rome but never ordered, so the JOIN finds nothing for him and he quietly disappears. Here that does not change Rome's total, but if the question were "how many customers per city", forgetting him would be wrong. That is why you check edge cases at the end.

In short: decide what one output row means, pick tables and keys, write the query, then ask who could be missing or counted twice.

sections.title: Query order
sections.summary: Why an alias in SELECT cannot be used in WHERE
sections.body:
**Question:** Customers whose total spend is above 100. Why does `WHERE spend > 100` fail?

SQL runs in this order: `FROM -> WHERE -> GROUP BY -> HAVING -> SELECT -> ORDER BY -> LIMIT`.

**Query:**
```sql
SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS spend
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING SUM(amount) > 100;
```

**Result:**

| customer_id | spend |
|---|---|
| 1 | 360 |

**Watch out:** WHERE runs before GROUP BY and SELECT, so it cannot see `spend` or any SUM. Filter groups with HAVING.

**Next question:** How do I just pick some rows and columns? -> [Basics](#sql-basics)
sections.explain:
Think of a kitchen. You first take the ingredients out of the fridge, then throw away the bad ones, then sort the rest into bowls, then throw away bowls that are too small, and only at the end write labels on the bowls. SQL works in the same order: FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY, LIMIT.

Walk through the card. FROM takes all 6 rows of `orders`. GROUP BY makes one pile per customer: customer 1 has 20, 300 and 40, customer 2 has 50 and 50, customer 3 has 10. The sums are 360, 100 and 10. HAVING keeps only piles with a sum above 100, so only customer 1 stays (100 is not above 100). Last, SELECT writes the label `spend` next to 360.

Why does `WHERE spend > 100` fail? WHERE works earlier, on single order rows, before any pile exists. At that moment there is no total and no label called `spend` yet, so the database cannot understand it.

In short: WHERE filters single rows before grouping, HAVING filters groups after grouping, and SELECT names come last.

sections.title: SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY
sections.summary: Pick rows and columns, sort, limit
sections.body:
**Question:** The 3 biggest orders of at least 20, biggest first.

**Query:**
```sql
SELECT order_id, amount
FROM orders
WHERE amount >= 20
ORDER BY amount DESC
LIMIT 3;
```

**Result:**

| order_id | amount |
|---|---|
| 102 | 300 |
| 103 | 50 |
| 106 | 50 |

**Watch out:** with `LIMIT 2` the two orders of 50 tie and the database may return either one. Add a second sort column (`ORDER BY amount DESC, order_id`) so the answer is always the same.

**Next question:** One total per customer instead of one row per order? -> [Aggregation](#sql-aggregation)
sections.explain:
You want the 3 biggest orders, but only orders of at least 20. The database does it in this order.

First FROM takes all 6 orders. Then WHERE checks each row one by one: is the amount 20 or more? Order 104 (10) fails and is thrown away. Five rows stay: 20, 300, 50, 40, 50. Then ORDER BY amount DESC sorts them from biggest to smallest: 300, 50, 50, 40, 20. Finally LIMIT 3 cuts the list after the third row, so you get 102 (300), 103 (50) and 106 (50).

The trap is a tie. Orders 103 and 106 both have 50. If you asked for only 2 rows, the database must choose one of the two 50s, and it has no rule for which one. Today you may get 103, tomorrow 106. It is like two runners finishing at the same time: someone must decide who is on the podium. Adding a second sort column, like `order_id`, is that rule: if amounts are equal, the smaller id comes first.

In short: WHERE removes rows, ORDER BY sorts what is left, LIMIT cuts the top, and a second sort column makes ties always come out the same.

sections.title: GROUP BY and aggregates
sections.summary: One summary row per group
sections.body:
**Question:** How many orders and how much money per customer?

**Query:**
```sql
SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS n_orders, SUM(amount) AS spend,
       AVG(amount) AS avg_order
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id;
```

**Result:**

| customer_id | n_orders | spend | avg_order |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 3 | 360 | 120 |
| 2 | 2 | 100 | 50 |
| 3 | 1 | 10 | 10 |

**Watch out:** every SELECT column must be in GROUP BY or inside an aggregate. Ana's average (120) is mostly the one 300 order.

**Next question:** The names live in `customers`. How do I bring them in? -> [Joins](#sql-joins)
sections.explain:
Imagine you pour all receipts on a table and make one pile per customer. That is GROUP BY. Then for each pile you count the receipts, add them up, and take the average. Those are COUNT, SUM and AVG.

With the card's data: Ana (customer 1) has receipts 20, 300 and 40. Count 3, sum 360, average 360 / 3 = 120. Ben (customer 2) has 50 and 50: count 2, sum 100, average 50. Cara (customer 3) has one receipt of 10: count 1, sum 10, average 10. Dan has no receipts in `orders`, so he gets no pile at all. Six rows went in, three summary rows came out.

The first trap: after grouping, each pile becomes ONE row. If you also ask for a column that is not the pile label and not a sum or count, like `order_date`, the database does not know which of Ana's three dates to show. So every column must be in GROUP BY or inside an aggregate.

The second trap: Ana's average of 120 looks like a typical order, but two of her three orders are only 20 and 40. The one 300 order raises the average a lot.

In short: GROUP BY makes piles, aggregates turn each pile into one number, and one big value can change an average a lot.

sections.title: INNER JOIN
sections.summary: Combine two tables on a key
sections.body:
**Question:** Show each order with the customer's name.

**Query:**
```sql
SELECT o.order_id, c.name, o.amount
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
ORDER BY o.order_id;
```

**Result:**

| order_id | name | amount |
|---|---|---|
| 101 | Ana | 20 |
| 102 | Ana | 300 |
| 103 | Ben | 50 |
| 104 | Cara | 10 |
| 105 | Ana | 40 |
| 106 | Ben | 50 |

**Watch out:** INNER JOIN keeps only matches. Dan has no orders, so he is gone. If the key repeats on both sides, rows multiply.

**Next question:** How do I keep Dan and show 0 for him? -> [LEFT JOIN and NULLs](#sql-left-join-nulls)
sections.explain:
The order list only has a `customer_id`, a number. To see the name, the database must look that number up in `customers`, like finding a name in a phone book by its number.

The JOIN takes each order and searches `customers` for the row with the same `customer_id`. Order 101 has customer 1, which is Ana, so the row becomes 101, Ana, 20. Order 103 has customer 2, so Ben. Order 104 has customer 3, so Cara. All 6 orders find a partner, so you get 6 rows. Then ORDER BY sorts them by order id.

Now look at who is missing. Dan is in `customers` but has no order, so no order ever points to him. An INNER JOIN keeps only pairs that match on both sides, so Dan never shows up.

The other trap is copies. If Ana were in `customers` twice by mistake, each of her 3 orders would match 2 rows, and you would get 6 Ana rows instead of 3. Any sum after that would be double.

In short: INNER JOIN glues matching rows together, drops anything without a partner, and multiplies rows when the key repeats.

sections.title: LEFT JOIN and NULLs
sections.summary: Keep every row of the left table, even without a match
sections.body:
**Question:** Spend per customer, including customers who never ordered (show 0).

**Query:**
```sql
SELECT c.name, COALESCE(SUM(o.amount), 0) AS spend
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
GROUP BY c.name
ORDER BY spend DESC;
```

**Result:**

| name | spend |
|---|---|
| Ana | 360 |
| Ben | 100 |
| Cara | 10 |
| Dan | 0 |

**Watch out:** a filter on the right table in WHERE (`WHERE o.amount > 10`) removes Dan again. Put it in the ON clause instead. Also `COUNT(o.order_id)` gives 0, `COUNT(*)` gives 1.

**Next question:** How do I label orders as small or big? -> [CASE WHEN](#sql-case-when)
sections.explain:
You want a list of ALL customers with their spend, even the ones who never bought. A LEFT JOIN keeps every row of the left table (`customers`) no matter what. When a customer has orders, they are glued on like a normal join. When he has none, the database still keeps him and fills the order columns with NULL, which means "empty, no value".

Step by step: Ana matches 3 orders, Ben 2, Cara 1, and Dan matches nothing, so he gets one row with an empty amount. GROUP BY name makes one pile per person. SUM gives 360, 100 and 10. For Dan, SUM of only empty values is NULL, and COALESCE replaces NULL with 0. Then the list is sorted by spend.

Why does `WHERE o.amount > 10` bring the problem back? WHERE runs after the join. Dan's amount is empty, and "empty > 10" is not true, so his row is thrown away. Putting the condition in ON instead means "only glue orders above 10", and Dan stays with an empty row.

Counting has the same idea: `COUNT(*)` counts Dan's row, so 1, while `COUNT(o.order_id)` skips empty values, so 0.

In short: LEFT JOIN keeps everyone on the left, fills missing matches with NULL, and a WHERE on the right table can silently remove them again.

sections.title: CASE WHEN
sections.summary: If/else inside a query: labels and conditional counts
sections.body:
**Question:** Label each order: under 50 is small, else big. Then count each label.

**Query:**
```sql
SELECT CASE WHEN amount < 50 THEN 'small' ELSE 'big' END AS size,
       COUNT(*) AS n
FROM orders
GROUP BY size;
```

**Result:**

| size | n |
|---|---|
| big | 3 |
| small | 3 |

Same trick for counts in one row: `SUM(CASE WHEN amount < 50 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)`.

**Watch out:** CASE stops at the first true branch, so order the branches from most specific. A missing ELSE gives NULL.

**Next question:** Which orders are above the average order? -> [Subqueries](#sql-subqueries)
sections.explain:
CASE WHEN is an "if, else" sentence inside the query. For each row it asks a question and writes a label.

Walk through the 6 orders. 20 is under 50, so "small". 300 is not, so "big". 50 is not under 50, so "big". 10 is "small". 40 is "small". The second 50 is "big". Now every row has a new column called `size`. Then GROUP BY size makes two piles, and COUNT counts each pile: 3 big (300, 50, 50) and 3 small (20, 10, 40).

The same idea can count without grouping: write 1 when the condition is true and 0 otherwise, then add the ones. That gives several counts in a single row.

Why does order matter? CASE reads the branches from top to bottom and stops at the first one that is true, like a guard who lets you in at the first door that opens. If you wrote "amount > 10 THEN medium" before "amount > 100 THEN huge", the 300 order would stop at "medium" and never reach "huge". So put the most specific test first. And if no branch is true and there is no ELSE, the label is NULL, an empty value.

In short: CASE gives each row a label by checking conditions in order, and you can then group or add those labels.

sections.title: Subqueries
sections.summary: Use the result of one query inside another
sections.body:
**Question:** Which orders are above the average order amount (78.3)?

**Query:**
```sql
SELECT order_id, amount
FROM orders
WHERE amount > (SELECT AVG(amount) FROM orders);
```

**Result:**

| order_id | amount |
|---|---|
| 102 | 300 |

**Watch out:** only the 300 order beats the average, because one huge value raises the average a lot. `IN (subquery)` with a NULL inside `NOT IN` returns nothing.

**Next question:** Nested queries get hard to read. Can I name each step? -> [CTEs](#sql-cte)
sections.explain:
You want the orders that are bigger than the average order. But the average is not written anywhere; you have to compute it first. A subquery is a small query inside the big one that does exactly this first job.

The database runs the inner part first: the average of 20, 300, 50, 10, 40 and 50 is 470 / 6, about 78.3. Now the outer query works like WHERE amount > 78.3. It checks every order: 20 no, 300 yes, 50 no, 10 no, 40 no, 50 no. Only order 102 stays.

Why only one? The single 300 order raises the average a lot. Without it, the average of the other five would be 34. So "above average" here really means "the giant order".

The second trap is NOT IN. `x NOT IN (1, 2, NULL)` means "x is not 1 and not 2 and not the empty value". The database cannot say whether x differs from an empty value, so the whole answer becomes "unknown" and no row is returned. Remove NULLs inside the subquery first, or use NOT EXISTS.

In short: a subquery computes a value first, then the outer query uses it like a normal number.

sections.title: CTE (WITH)
sections.summary: Name a step, then query it like a table
sections.body:
**Question:** Customers who spent more than the average customer.

**Query:**
```sql
WITH spend AS (
  SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS total
  FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT customer_id, total
FROM spend
WHERE total > (SELECT AVG(total) FROM spend);
```

**Result:**

| customer_id | total |
|---|---|
| 1 | 360 |

**Watch out:** average per customer (Ana 360, Ben 100, Cara 10: avg 156.7) is not the average per order (78.3). Say which one the question means.

**Next question:** How much did we sell each month? -> [Dates](#sql-dates)
sections.explain:
A CTE is like writing an intermediate result on a separate sheet of paper and giving the sheet a name. WITH spend AS (...) means "first make a small table called `spend`, then use it below".

Step 1, the named sheet: group `orders` by customer and add the amounts. Ana 360, Ben 100, Cara 10. This little table has 3 rows.

Step 2, the main query reads `spend` like any table. It computes the average of the 3 totals: (360 + 100 + 10) / 3, about 156.7. Then it keeps customers whose total is above that. Ana's 360 passes, Ben's 100 and Cara's 10 do not.

The trap is which average. The average per customer is 156.7, because there are 3 customers. The average per order is 470 / 6, about 78.3, because there are 6 orders. With the per order number, Ben's 100 would also pass, and you would get a different answer. Both sound like "the average", so say which one the question means.

A CTE also makes long queries readable: each step has a name, you read top to bottom instead of inside out.

In short: WITH names a step so you can reuse it, and the average per customer is not the same as the average per order.

sections.title: Dates
sections.summary: Group by month, filter a date range
sections.body:
**Question:** Revenue per month in Q1 2024.

**Query:**
```sql
SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', order_date) AS month, SUM(amount) AS revenue
FROM orders
WHERE order_date >= '2024-01-01' AND order_date < '2024-04-01'
GROUP BY month
ORDER BY month;
```

**Result:**

| month | revenue |
|---|---|
| 2024-01 | 70 |
| 2024-02 | 310 |
| 2024-03 | 90 |

**Watch out:** use `>= start AND < next day` instead of BETWEEN with timestamps, or you lose the last day after 00:00. Function names differ: Postgres uses `DATE_TRUNC('month', d)`.

**Next question:** Rank customers by spend without losing rows? -> [Window ranking](#sql-window-ranking)
sections.explain:
You want one number per month. The dates are full days like 2024-02-15, so first the database turns each date into just its month, like putting every receipt into a monthly folder.

Step by step: WHERE keeps dates from 2024-01-01 up to, but not including, 2024-04-01. All 6 orders pass. Then `strftime('%Y-%m', ...)` turns each date into "2024-01", "2024-02" or "2024-03". GROUP BY month makes three folders. SUM adds each one: January 20 + 50 = 70, February 300 + 10 = 310, March 50 + 40 = 90. ORDER BY month puts them in calendar order.

Why `< 2024-04-01` and not BETWEEN up to 2024-03-31? Real data often stores a time too, like "2024-03-31 14:00". To the database that is later than "2024-03-31", which means midnight at the start of that day. So BETWEEN would drop every order made on March 31 after midnight. "Smaller than the first day of the next month" catches the whole last day.

Also, each database names its date functions differently, so in Postgres you would write `DATE_TRUNC('month', d)` instead.

In short: turn each date into its month, group by it, and filter ranges with "from start, up to but not including the next start".

sections.title: ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK
sections.summary: Rank rows without collapsing them
sections.body:
**Question:** Rank orders by amount. What happens to the two orders of 50?

**Query:**
```sql
SELECT order_id, amount,
  ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC) AS rn,
  RANK()       OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC) AS rnk,
  DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC) AS drnk
FROM orders;
```

**Result:**

| order_id | amount | rn | rnk | drnk |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 102 | 300 | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| 103 | 50 | 2 | 2 | 2 |
| 106 | 50 | 3 | 2 | 2 |
| 105 | 40 | 4 | 4 | 3 |
| 101 | 20 | 5 | 5 | 4 |
| 104 | 10 | 6 | 6 | 5 |

**Watch out:** the two 50s tie: ROW_NUMBER gives them 2 and 3 (in any order), RANK gives 2, 2 then skips to 4, DENSE_RANK gives 2, 2 then 3. Say which one you chose and why.

**Next question:** The biggest order of EACH customer? -> [Top N per group](#sql-top-n)
sections.explain:
Think of a race. You want to give places, but you do not want to merge runners together like GROUP BY would. A window function adds a new column to every row while keeping all rows. OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC) means "line the orders up from biggest to smallest and look at the line".

The line is: 300, 50, 50, 40, 20, 10. Now three ways to number it.

ROW_NUMBER just counts 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. The two 50s get 2 and 3, and which one gets 2 is a coin flip.

RANK says tied runners share a place: both 50s are 2. But two people used places 2 and 3, so the next one, 40, gets place 4. Place 3 is skipped, like in sports.

DENSE_RANK also gives both 50s place 2, but does not skip: 40 gets 3, 20 gets 4, 10 gets 5.

Which to choose? ROW_NUMBER when you need exactly one row per place (for example, exactly one winner). RANK or DENSE_RANK when ties should be treated fairly. The difference only shows when there is a tie, which is why the card uses the two 50s.

In short: all three number rows in order without removing any; they only differ in how they handle ties.

sections.title: Top N per group
sections.summary: Best row(s) inside each group
sections.body:
**Question:** The biggest order of each customer.

**Query:**
```sql
WITH r AS (
  SELECT customer_id, order_id, amount,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY amount DESC) AS rn
  FROM orders
)
SELECT customer_id, order_id, amount FROM r WHERE rn = 1;
```

**Result:**

| customer_id | order_id | amount |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 102 | 300 |
| 2 | 103 | 50 |
| 3 | 104 | 10 |

**Watch out:** you cannot use `rn` in WHERE of the same query (it is computed in SELECT), so wrap it in a CTE. Use RANK if ties should all be kept.

**Next question:** How many days between a customer's orders? -> [LAG and LEAD](#sql-lag-lead)
sections.explain:
You want the biggest order of EACH customer, not of the whole shop. So you need a ranking that starts over for every customer, like each class having its own best student.

PARTITION BY customer_id splits the orders into one small line per customer, and ORDER BY amount DESC sorts each line from biggest to smallest. ROW_NUMBER then counts inside each line. Ana's line is 300, 40, 20, numbered 1, 2, 3. Ben's line is 50, 50, numbered 1 and 2. Cara has only 10, numbered 1. Then the outer query keeps rows with number 1: Ana's 300, one of Ben's 50s, Cara's 10.

Why the CTE? The number `rn` is created in SELECT, and WHERE runs before SELECT, so WHERE cannot see it in the same query. Putting the ranking in a named step first, then filtering, solves it.

Ben's two orders tie at 50. ROW_NUMBER must still give 1 and 2, so it picks one of them, here order 103. If the question wants every tied best order, use RANK: both 50s would get 1 and both would stay.

In short: PARTITION BY restarts the count for each group, then keep number 1 in an outer step.

sections.title: LAG and LEAD
sections.summary: Compare a row with the previous or next row
sections.body:
**Question:** For each order, how many days since the same customer's previous order?

**Query:**
```sql
SELECT customer_id, order_date,
  LAG(order_date) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date) AS prev,
  julianday(order_date) - julianday(LAG(order_date)
    OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date)) AS days_gap
FROM orders
ORDER BY customer_id, order_date;
```

**Result:**

| customer_id | order_date | prev | days_gap |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 2024-01-10 | NULL | NULL |
| 1 | 2024-02-15 | 2024-01-10 | 36 |
| 1 | 2024-03-20 | 2024-02-15 | 34 |
| 2 | 2024-01-25 | NULL | NULL |
| 2 | 2024-03-02 | 2024-01-25 | 37 |
| 3 | 2024-02-12 | NULL | NULL |

**Watch out:** the first order of each customer has no previous one, so it is NULL. Forget PARTITION BY and you compare different customers.

**Next question:** Total sales so far, day by day? -> [Running totals](#sql-running-totals)
sections.explain:
You want to compare each order with the one just before it from the same customer. LAG means "look one row back". LEAD means "look one row forward".

First the database lines the orders up per customer (PARTITION BY customer_id) and by date (ORDER BY order_date). Ana's line is Jan 10, Feb 15, Mar 20. Ben's line is Jan 25, Mar 2. Cara's line is only Feb 12.

Then LAG fills a `prev` column with the date of the row above in the same line. Ana's first order has nobody above, so `prev` is NULL (empty). Her second gets Jan 10, her third gets Feb 15. The gap is the date minus the previous date: Jan 10 to Feb 15 is 36 days, Feb 15 to Mar 20 is 34 days (2024 has a 29 day February). Ben: Jan 25 to Mar 2 is 37 days. Cara has one order, so NULL.

Why is PARTITION BY so important? Without it, all orders form one line by date, and Ben's Jan 25 order would look back at Ana's Jan 10 order. You would measure the gap between two different people, which means nothing.

In short: LAG peeks at the previous row in each customer's own line, and the first row has nothing before it, so it is NULL.

sections.title: Running totals
sections.summary: Cumulative sum with a window
sections.body:
**Question:** Revenue so far after each order date.

**Query:**
```sql
SELECT order_date, amount,
  SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY order_date
                    ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS running
FROM orders
ORDER BY order_date;
```

**Result:**

| order_date | amount | running |
|---|---|---|
| 2024-01-10 | 20 | 20 |
| 2024-01-25 | 50 | 70 |
| 2024-02-12 | 10 | 80 |
| 2024-02-15 | 300 | 380 |
| 2024-03-02 | 50 | 430 |
| 2024-03-20 | 40 | 470 |

**Watch out:** without the ROWS clause the default is RANGE, so rows with the same date get the same total at once. For a 7-day moving average use `ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` on daily rows.

**Next question:** Which customers live in the same city as each other? -> [Self join](#sql-self-join)
sections.explain:
A running total is like a piggy bank: after each coin you write down how much is inside now.

The database lines the orders up by date, then for each row adds everything from the first row down to this row. That is what "ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW" says: from the very top to me.

Walk through it. Jan 10: 20, so the total is 20. Jan 25: 50, total 70. Feb 12: 10, total 80. Feb 15: 300, total 380. Mar 2: 50, total 430. Mar 20: 40, total 470. The last number equals the total of all orders, which is a nice check.

Why write the ROWS part? If you leave it out, the default treats all rows with the same date as one block. If two orders happened on the same day, both rows would show the total after BOTH orders, instead of growing one step at a time. Here every date is different, so you see no change, but on real data you would.

The same frame idea gives moving averages: "6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW" means this row plus the 6 before it, so 7 days if there is one row per day.

In short: a running total adds every earlier row plus the current one, and ROWS makes it grow exactly one row at a time.

sections.title: Self join
sections.summary: Join a table to itself to compare rows
sections.body:
**Question:** List pairs of customers who live in the same city.

**Query:**
```sql
SELECT a.name AS cust_a, b.name AS cust_b, a.city
FROM customers a
JOIN customers b
  ON a.city = b.city AND a.customer_id < b.customer_id;
```

**Result:**

| cust_a | cust_b | city |
|---|---|---|
| Ana | Cara | Paris |
| Ben | Dan | Rome |

**Watch out:** with `<>` instead of `<` every pair shows twice (Ana-Cara and Cara-Ana). Use `<` to keep each pair once.

**Next question:** Did customers come back the month after they signed up? -> [Retention](#sql-retention)
sections.explain:
To compare customers with other customers, you need two copies of the same list side by side. A self join does that: the table is used twice, with two nicknames, `a` and `b`.

The database tries every pair of a row from `a` and a row from `b`, and keeps pairs where the city is the same. In Paris there are Ana (1) and Cara (3), so the same city pairs are Ana-Ana, Ana-Cara, Cara-Ana and Cara-Cara. In Rome, with Ben (2) and Dan (4), you get Ben-Ben, Ben-Dan, Dan-Ben and Dan-Dan.

Now the extra rule `a.customer_id < b.customer_id`. Ana-Ana fails (1 is not smaller than 1), so a person is never paired with herself. Ana-Cara passes (1 < 3), but Cara-Ana fails (3 < 1 is false). So each pair appears once: Ana-Cara and Ben-Dan.

With `<>` (not equal) instead, the self pairs are gone, but both Ana-Cara and Cara-Ana pass, so every pair shows twice. It is like a handshake: Ana shaking Cara's hand is the same handshake as Cara shaking Ana's.

In short: a self join puts the table next to itself, and `<` on the id keeps each pair exactly once.

sections.title: Retention
sections.summary: Who comes back after the first period
sections.body:
**Question:** Of customers who ordered in January, how many ordered again in February or later?

**Query:**
```sql
WITH first AS (
  SELECT customer_id, MIN(order_date) AS first_order
  FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', f.first_order) AS cohort,
  COUNT(DISTINCT f.customer_id) AS customers,
  COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN strftime('%Y-%m', o.order_date) >
        strftime('%Y-%m', f.first_order) THEN o.customer_id END) AS came_back
FROM first f JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = f.customer_id
GROUP BY cohort;
```

**Result:**

| cohort | customers | came_back |
|---|---|---|
| 2024-01 | 2 | 2 |
| 2024-02 | 1 | 0 |

January cohort: Ana and Ben, both came back (2 of 2). February cohort: Cara, no later order.

**Watch out:** the cohort is the month of the FIRST order, not of any order. Count DISTINCT customers, not orders.

**Next question:** How many people go from view to cart to buy? -> [Funnels](#sql-funnels)
sections.explain:
Retention asks: of the people who started in a month, how many came back later? First you need each customer's start month, called their cohort, like the year a student joined school.

Step 1, the CTE `first`: for each customer, the earliest order date. Ana Jan 10, Ben Jan 25, Cara Feb 12. So Ana and Ben are the January cohort, Cara is February.

Step 2: join this back to all orders, so each order knows its customer's start month. Ana has 3 rows, Ben 2, Cara 1. For each row the CASE asks: is this order's month later than the start month? Ana's February and March orders say yes, Ben's March order says yes, Cara's only order says no. A "no" gives NULL, which is not counted.

Step 3: group by cohort. January: 2 different customers, and 2 different customers with a later order. Ana had two later orders but DISTINCT counts her once. February: 1 customer, 0 came back.

The traps: the cohort must come from the FIRST order, otherwise Ana would sit in three cohorts. And count people, not orders, or Ana alone would look like 2 returns.

In short: find each person's first month, then count how many different people ordered again in a later month.

sections.title: Funnels
sections.summary: How many people reach each step
sections.body:
**Question:** How many customers reached each step: view, cart, buy?

`events`

| customer_id | step |
|---|---|
| 1 | view |
| 1 | cart |
| 1 | buy |
| 2 | view |
| 2 | cart |
| 3 | view |
| 4 | view |

**Query:**
```sql
SELECT
  COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN step = 'view' THEN customer_id END) AS viewed,
  COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN step = 'cart' THEN customer_id END) AS carted,
  COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN step = 'buy'  THEN customer_id END) AS bought
FROM events;
```

**Result:**

| viewed | carted | bought |
|---|---|---|
| 4 | 2 | 1 |

**Watch out:** a strict funnel only counts `cart` if the same person also viewed (and before buy). Mention the order in time if the table has timestamps.

**Next question:** What share of viewers bought? -> [Ratios](#sql-ratios)
sections.explain:
A funnel is like a shop with three doors: look, put in the basket, pay. Fewer people get through each door. You want to know how many reach each one.

The `events` table has one row per step a person did. The query reads every row once. For the `viewed` column, CASE writes the customer id if the step is "view" and leaves it empty (NULL) otherwise. COUNT DISTINCT then counts the different ids and ignores the empty ones. Views come from customers 1, 2, 3 and 4, so 4. Cart rows come from 1 and 2, so 2. Buy comes only from 1, so 1. The result is one row: 4, 2, 1. From that you can say half of viewers added to cart and half of those bought.

DISTINCT matters because a person could view ten times; they are still one person.

The trap: this simple version counts each step on its own. If someone had a "buy" row with no "cart" row (a data error, or buying directly), they would still be counted as a buyer. A strict funnel only counts a step if the same person did the previous step first, which needs timestamps to check the order.

In short: count different people at each step, and decide whether a later step requires the earlier steps.

sections.title: Ratios and percentages
sections.summary: Share of a total, without integer division
sections.body:
**Question:** What share of all revenue comes from each city?

**Query:**
```sql
SELECT c.city, SUM(o.amount) AS revenue,
  ROUND(100.0 * SUM(o.amount) / (SELECT SUM(amount) FROM orders), 1) AS pct
FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
GROUP BY c.city;
```

**Result:**

| city | revenue | pct |
|---|---|---|
| Paris | 370 | 78.7 |
| Rome | 100 | 21.3 |

**Watch out:** `100 * a / b` with integers rounds down (in SQLite and Postgres 1/4 = 0). Multiply by `100.0` first. Guard against 0 with `NULLIF(b, 0)`.

**Next question:** How do I find streaks of days in a row? -> [Gaps and islands](#sql-gaps-islands)
sections.explain:
You want each city's piece of the whole cake in percent. That means city revenue divided by total revenue, times 100.

Step by step: the JOIN gives each order its city. GROUP BY city adds them: Paris 370, Rome 100. The small subquery computes the total of all orders, 470. Then for Paris: 100.0 times 370 divided by 470 is about 78.72, rounded to 78.7. For Rome: 100.0 times 100 divided by 470 is about 21.28, so 21.3. The two add up to 100, a good check.

Why `100.0` and not `100`? When both numbers are whole numbers, many databases do whole number division and just cut off the decimals. 370 / 470 would give 0, not 0.787, and your Paris share would be 0 percent. Writing 100.0 first makes the database use decimals from the start.

And dividing by zero is an error. `NULLIF(b, 0)` means "if b is 0, treat it as empty". Dividing by an empty value gives an empty result instead of crashing.

In short: share = part / total times 100, written with 100.0 so decimals are kept, and protected against a total of 0.

sections.title: Gaps and islands
sections.summary: Find streaks of consecutive days
sections.body:
**Question:** Ana visited on these days. What are her streaks of days in a row?

`visits`

| customer_id | visit_date |
|---|---|
| 1 | 2024-03-01 |
| 1 | 2024-03-02 |
| 1 | 2024-03-03 |
| 1 | 2024-03-07 |
| 1 | 2024-03-08 |

**Query:**
```sql
WITH g AS (
  SELECT visit_date,
    julianday(visit_date)
      - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY visit_date) AS grp
  FROM visits
)
SELECT MIN(visit_date) AS start, MAX(visit_date) AS finish, COUNT(*) AS days
FROM g GROUP BY grp ORDER BY start;
```

**Result:**

| start | finish | days |
|---|---|---|
| 2024-03-01 | 2024-03-03 | 3 |
| 2024-03-07 | 2024-03-08 | 2 |

**Watch out:** the trick: date minus row number is the same for every day in one streak. Remove duplicate days first, or the row number breaks the streak.

**Next question:** The data has the same order loaded twice. How do I keep one? -> [Dedup and cleaning](#sql-dedup-cleaning)
sections.explain:
Ana visited on March 1, 2, 3, then 7, 8. You want to see the two streaks: 1 to 3 and 7 to 8. The trick needs one clever subtraction.

Step 1: sort the visits by date and number them: March 1 is 1, March 2 is 2, March 3 is 3, March 7 is 4, March 8 is 5.

Step 2: subtract the number from the day. March 1 minus 1 is 0, March 2 minus 2 is 0, March 3 minus 3 is 0. March 7 minus 4 is 3, March 8 minus 5 is 3. Inside a streak, the date and the counter both go up by 1 each step, so their difference stays the same. When a day is skipped, the date jumps but the counter does not, so the difference changes. That difference becomes a group label.

Step 3: group by that label. Group 0: first day March 1, last day March 3, 3 days. Group 3: March 7 to March 8, 2 days.

The trap: if March 2 appeared twice, the counter would go up without the date going up, the difference would drop, and one streak would split in two. Remove duplicate days first.

In short: date minus row number stays constant inside a streak, so you can group by it.

sections.title: Dedup and cleaning
sections.summary: Keep one row per key
sections.body:
**Question:** Order 101 was loaded twice. Keep only the latest load of each order.

`orders_raw`

| order_id | customer_id | amount | loaded_at |
|---|---|---|---|
| 101 | 1 | 20 | 09:00 |
| 101 | 1 | 20 | 09:05 |
| 103 | 2 | 50 | 09:00 |
| 104 | 3 | 10 | 09:00 |

**Query:**
```sql
WITH r AS (
  SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY order_id
                               ORDER BY loaded_at DESC) AS rn
  FROM orders_raw
)
SELECT order_id, customer_id, amount, loaded_at FROM r WHERE rn = 1;
```

**Result:**

| order_id | customer_id | amount | loaded_at |
|---|---|---|---|
| 101 | 1 | 20 | 09:05 |
| 103 | 2 | 50 | 09:00 |
| 104 | 3 | 10 | 09:00 |

**Watch out:** `SELECT DISTINCT` only removes rows that are identical in EVERY column. Here the load time differs, so use ROW_NUMBER. Also clean text (`TRIM`, `LOWER`) before comparing.

**Next question:** Revenue per city as columns, one column per month? -> [Pivot](#sql-pivot)
sections.explain:
Order 101 was loaded twice, at 09:00 and 09:05. You want one row per order, the latest one.

Step 1: PARTITION BY order_id puts the rows of each order in their own small line, and ORDER BY loaded_at DESC puts the newest load first. ROW_NUMBER numbers each line. Order 101: the 09:05 row gets 1, the 09:00 row gets 2. Orders 103 and 104 have one row each, so they get 1.

Step 2: the outer query keeps only rows numbered 1. You get 101 at 09:05, 103 and 104. The old copy of 101 is gone.

Why not just SELECT DISTINCT? DISTINCT only removes rows that are identical in every single column, like two photocopies of the same page. Here the two rows of 101 differ in `loaded_at`, so to DISTINCT they are two different rows and both stay. ROW_NUMBER lets you say "same order id is a duplicate, and keep the newest".

A related trap: "Paris" and " paris" look the same to you but not to the database. Clean the text with TRIM (remove spaces at the ends) and LOWER (make all letters small) before comparing.

In short: number the rows inside each key, newest first, and keep number 1.

sections.title: Pivot
sections.summary: Turn row values into columns
sections.body:
**Question:** One row per city, one column per month of revenue.

**Query:**
```sql
SELECT c.city,
  SUM(CASE WHEN strftime('%m', o.order_date) = '01' THEN o.amount ELSE 0 END) AS jan,
  SUM(CASE WHEN strftime('%m', o.order_date) = '02' THEN o.amount ELSE 0 END) AS feb,
  SUM(CASE WHEN strftime('%m', o.order_date) = '03' THEN o.amount ELSE 0 END) AS mar
FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
GROUP BY c.city;
```

**Result:**

| city | jan | feb | mar |
|---|---|---|---|
| Paris | 20 | 310 | 40 |
| Rome | 50 | 0 | 50 |

**Watch out:** SQL needs the columns written by hand. Without `ELSE 0` empty cells are NULL.

**Next question:** The typical order, not pulled up by the 300? -> [Median and percentiles](#sql-median-percentiles)
sections.explain:
A pivot turns a long list into a wide grid, like a school timetable: one row per city, one column per month.

Step 1: the JOIN gives each order its city. Step 2: for the `jan` column, CASE looks at every order and says: if the month is 01, use the amount, else use 0. The same for `feb` and `mar`. So each order puts its money into exactly one of the three columns and 0 into the other two. Step 3: GROUP BY city adds the columns per city.

Paris has Ana's 20 (January), 300 (February) and 40 (March), plus Cara's 10 (February). So Paris is 20, 310, 40. Rome has Ben's 50 in January and 50 in March, and nothing in February, so 50, 0, 50.

Why do you write each column by hand? SQL must know all output columns before it reads the data, so it cannot create a column for "every month that exists". You list them yourself.

Why ELSE 0? Without it, a non matching row gives NULL (empty) instead of 0. Rome has no February orders, so all its February values are empty, and the sum of only empty values is NULL, not 0.

In short: one CASE per column sends each amount to the right month, then GROUP BY adds them up.

sections.title: Median and percentiles
sections.summary: Middle value that one huge order cannot move much
sections.body:
**Question:** What is the median order amount? (The average is 78.3 because of the 300 order.)

**Query:**
```sql
WITH r AS (
  SELECT amount,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY amount) AS rn,
    COUNT(*) OVER () AS n
  FROM orders
)
SELECT AVG(amount) AS median
FROM r WHERE rn IN ((n + 1) / 2, (n + 2) / 2);
```

**Result:**

| median |
|---|
| 45 |

**Watch out:** with an even count the median is the average of the two middle values (here 40 and 50). Postgres has `PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY amount)`; SQLite and MySQL do not.

**Next question:** A manager chain of any depth, or a list of every day? -> [Recursive CTE](#sql-recursive-cte)
sections.explain:
The average order is 78.3, but that is mostly the one 300 order. The median is the middle value when you line the orders up from small to big, so one giant order cannot move it much.

Step 1: sort the amounts: 10, 20, 40, 50, 50, 300. ROW_NUMBER gives positions 1 to 6. `COUNT(*) OVER ()` writes the total count, 6, on every row, so each row knows how many there are.

Step 2: find the middle. With 6 values there is no single middle; there are two, positions 3 and 4. The formulas (n + 1) / 2 and (n + 2) / 2 give 7 / 2 and 8 / 2. With whole number division 7 / 2 is 3, so the positions are 3 and 4. With an odd count like 5, both formulas give 3, the one true middle.

Step 3: average the chosen rows: positions 3 and 4 hold 40 and 50, so the median is 45.

Compare: average 78.3, median 45. If the 300 became 3000, the average would jump to about 528, but the median would stay 45.

Postgres has a ready function for this, PERCENTILE_CONT; SQLite and MySQL do not, so you use the counting trick.

In short: sort, find the middle position (or the two middle ones), and average them.

sections.title: Recursive CTE
sections.summary: Walk a chain of any length, or make a list of dates
sections.body:
**Question:** Who reports to Eva, directly or through others, and at what level?

`staff`

| staff_id | name | manager_id |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Eva | NULL |
| 2 | Finn | 1 |
| 3 | Gus | 2 |
| 4 | Hana | 2 |

**Query:**
```sql
WITH RECURSIVE chain AS (
  SELECT staff_id, name, 0 AS level FROM staff WHERE manager_id IS NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT s.staff_id, s.name, c.level + 1
  FROM staff s JOIN chain c ON s.manager_id = c.staff_id
)
SELECT name, level FROM chain ORDER BY level, name;
```

**Result:**

| name | level |
|---|---|
| Eva | 0 |
| Finn | 1 |
| Gus | 2 |
| Hana | 2 |

Same pattern makes a calendar of all days, so days with no orders show 0 after a LEFT JOIN.

**Watch out:** always have a stop condition (the join runs out of rows, or `WHERE d < '2024-03-31'` when you generate dates), or the query never ends.

**Next question:** How do I do all of this in pandas? -> [SQL to pandas](#sql-pandas-equivalents)
sections.explain:
You want everyone under Eva, at any depth. A normal join goes only one level down. A recursive CTE repeats the join until nobody new is found, like asking "who reports to you?" and then asking each of those people the same question.

Step 1, the starting row: the person with no manager. That is Eva, level 0.

Step 2, repeat: find staff whose manager is someone found in the last round. Round 1: Finn's manager is 1 (Eva), so Finn is added at level 1. Round 2: Gus and Hana both have manager 2 (Finn), so they are added at level 2. Round 3: does anyone have manager 3 or 4? No. The round adds nothing, so the database stops.

UNION ALL stacks all rounds into one list: Eva 0, Finn 1, Gus 2, Hana 2.

The same idea builds a calendar: start with one day, then repeat "add one day" until a last date. Joining orders to this calendar with a LEFT JOIN shows days with no orders as 0.

The trap is the stop. The staff example stops by itself because the chain ends. The calendar has no natural end, so you must add a condition like "only while the date is before March 31", or it runs forever.

In short: start with a first row, keep adding the next level from the previous one, and make sure it stops.

sections.title: SQL to pandas
sections.summary: The same patterns in pandas
sections.body:
**Question:** The exam lets you use pandas instead of SQL. How does each SQL step translate?

| SQL | pandas (`o` = orders, `c` = customers) |
|---|---|
| `WHERE amount >= 20` | `o[o.amount >= 20]` |
| `GROUP BY customer_id, SUM(amount)` | `o.groupby('customer_id', as_index=False)['amount'].sum()` |
| `HAVING SUM(amount) > 100` | `s[s.amount > 100]` after the groupby |
| `LEFT JOIN customers` | `c.merge(o, on='customer_id', how='left')` |
| `COALESCE(x, 0)` | `.fillna(0)` |
| `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY amount DESC)` | `o.groupby('customer_id')['amount'].rank(method='first', ascending=False)` |
| `LAG(order_date) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ...)` | `o.sort_values('order_date').groupby('customer_id')['order_date'].shift()` |
| running `SUM() OVER (ORDER BY order_date)` | `o.sort_values('order_date')['amount'].cumsum()` |
| pivot with `SUM(CASE ...)` | `pd.pivot_table(df, index='city', columns='month', values='amount', aggfunc='sum', fill_value=0)` |
| dedup with ROW_NUMBER | `o.sort_values('loaded_at').drop_duplicates('order_id', keep='last')` |

**Watch out:** `groupby` drops NULL keys by default (`dropna=False` keeps them), and `merge` multiplies rows when the key repeats, like a JOIN.

**Next question:** All syntax on one page -> [SQL cheat sheet](#cheat-sql)
sections.explain:
pandas does the same jobs as SQL, just with Python words. Think of it as the same recipe written in another language.

WHERE becomes a mask: `o[o.amount >= 20]` keeps the rows where the test is true. GROUP BY with SUM becomes `groupby(...).sum()`: same piles, same totals (Ana 360, Ben 100, Cara 10). HAVING is just another mask applied to that small result. LEFT JOIN becomes `merge(..., how='left')`, and missing values appear as NaN, the pandas name for NULL, which `fillna(0)` turns into 0 for Dan. ROW_NUMBER per customer becomes `rank(method='first')` inside a groupby. LAG becomes `shift()`: sort by date, then each row gets the value of the row above in its group. A running total is `cumsum()`. A pivot is `pivot_table` with `fill_value=0`. Dedup is sort by load time and `drop_duplicates(..., keep='last')`.

Two traps carry over. First, `groupby` quietly drops rows whose group key is empty, so a customer with no id would vanish from the totals unless you add `dropna=False`. Second, `merge` behaves like a JOIN: if a key appears twice on one side, rows multiply, and sums become too big.

In short: every SQL step has a pandas twin, and the same traps (empty keys, repeated keys) apply.
